item.title: Transforming spinel LiMn2O4 into a Na-layered cathode
item.dc:creator: Zixin Wu
Diancheng Chen
Ting Lin
Maolin Yang
Chunjing Hu
Dian Zhang
Leiyu Chen

item.description:
Authors: Zixin Wu, Diancheng Chen, Ting Lin, Maolin Yang, Chunjing Hu, Dian Zhang, Leiyu Chen, Yonglin Tang, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The positive electrode structures of practical sodium-ion batteries are generally confined to polyanionic or layered transition metal oxide frameworks, where the trade-off between specific energy and structural stability limits their application. As a well-established positive electrode structure in lithium-ion batteries, the spinel framework has abundant storage sites for alkali metal ions, but it has received less attention for sodium-ion batteries. Here we show that spinel LiMn 2 O 4 can be transformed into a sodium-ion positive electrode. Electrochemical sodiation drives Mn-ion migration along an octahedral–tetrahedral–octahedral pathway, creating a layered/spinel heterostructure for further sodium storage. Moreover, residual spinel domains inhibit the strain and structural degradation within the layered structure. Consequently, a 26650 cylindrical cell using a LiMn 2 O 4 -derived sodium-ion positive electrode achieves a capacity of 3.85 Ah and retains 95.7% capacity after 900 cycles (1.925 A). This work demonstrates that spinel LiMn 2 O 4 can serve as a viable positive electrode for sodium-ion batteries, and that electrochemical transformation is a feasible approach for creating positive electrode frameworks.

item.title: Lipid droplets amplify inflammasome-driven cytokine secretion in infection and inflammation
item.dc:creator: Laura Pedró-Cos
Corentin Mallet
Fabien Thery
Paul Courrieu
Julien Pichon
Aude Remot
Denzel Eggermont
Florence Bugault
item.description:
Authors: Laura Pedró-Cos, Corentin Mallet, Fabien Thery, Paul Courrieu, Julien Pichon, Aude Remot, Denzel Eggermont, Florence Bugault, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Lipid droplets (LDs) accumulating in infected cells are traditionally viewed as passive nutrient stores exploited by invading pathogens. Here, we show that during infection with virulent Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), but not BCG, host LDs orchestrate protective immune responses by bridging the ISGylation and inflammasome pathways. Proteomic and imaging analyses reveal the selective recruitment of ISGylated proteins together with caspase-1 and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) precursors to the LD surface. Comparative LD proteomics in wild-type and ISG15-deficient macrophages, combined with ISGylome profiling, identify ISGylated proteins as mediators of pro-IL-1β binding to LDs. Functionally, disruption of LD biogenesis in primary human macrophages impairs mature IL-1β secretion and compromises Mtb control. Notably, this LD-dependent amplification of IL-1β release is not restricted to microbial stimuli but also occurs in response to sterile inflammasome activation. Collectively, these findings redefine LDs as immunoactive organelles integrating microbial and danger signals to potentiate inflammasome-dependent IL-1β responses during infection and inflammation.

item.title: Population-level characterisation of the human gut phageome and its association with microbial metabolites
item.dc:creator: Panayiotis Louca
Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei
Afroditi Kouraki
Erfan Khamespanah
Yu Lin
Xue Peng
Robert Pope
Alessia Visconti
item.description:
Authors: Panayiotis Louca, Mohammadali Khan Mirzaei, Afroditi Kouraki, Erfan Khamespanah, Yu Lin, Xue Peng, Robert Pope, Alessia Visconti, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11417
Abstract: Abstract Bacteriophages, viruses infecting bacteria, are abundant in the human gut, but their population-level structure and metabolic associations remain unclear Here we present a foundational characterisation of the gut phageome using deep shotgun metagenomic data in a large population-based cohort ( n = 1,069: TwinsUK). We assembled 116,740 non-redundant vOTUs of which 52.9% were predicted to be temperate and 47.0% virulent. Individuals harboured an average of 3,370 vOTUs, mostly at low abundances, exhibiting structured population-level co-abundance patterns with bacterial species including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Blautia wexlerae . Phageome diversity was mostly driven by environmental factors, with modest heritable components. We detected 4 significant vOTU diet associations. Additionally, 6,572 phages were associated with short-chain fatty acids and secondary bile acids, identifying extensive population-level associations between phage-associated genomic variation and microbial metabolites. Over 100 vOTUs encoded auxiliary metabolic genes, while a distinct subset of phages encoded virulence-associated genes, including vacuolating autotransporter toxin (vat) and LPS glucosyltransferases (gtrA, gtrB, gtr) implicated in O-antigen modification and immune invasion, and showed consistent co-abundance patterns with bacterial species previously associated with opportunistic or pathobiont features. These results identify structured population-level associations between phage-associated genomic elements, bacterial communities, and microbial metabolites, motivating future experimental and mechanistic studies.

item.title: Partially functional hypomorphic missense variants in BRCA2 are reduced penetrance pathogenic variants
item.dc:creator: Huaizhi Huang
Chunling Hu
Jie Na
Lisa N. Heppler
Andrew Goldfarb
Matthew Kucera
Timothy Simmons
Kevin L. Peterson
item.description:
Authors: Huaizhi Huang, Chunling Hu, Jie Na, Lisa N. Heppler, Andrew Goldfarb, Matthew Kucera, Timothy Simmons, Kevin L. Peterson, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11570
Abstract: Abstract Identification of partial loss-of-function (hypomorphic), reduced penetrance pathogenic missense variants (RPPVs) and assessment of the clinical relevance of these variants is needed for improved hereditary cancer risk estimation. Here we show that 70 candidate hypomorphic missense variants in the DNA-binding domain of BRCA2 reduce homologous recombination DNA repair activity and endogenous cell survival, decrease RAD51 foci formation, and increase sensitivity to Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors. The 34 “strong” hypomorphs with greatest effects on function are associated with moderate risks of female breast cancer and later ages of diagnosis than pathogenic variants (PVs), and 14 of these variants can be classified as “likely pathogenic” by integration of functional data into a ClinGen BRCA1/2 variant curation model. In addition, 32% of tumors with hypomorphic variants and corresponding loss of heterozygosity for BRCA2 display homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) compared to 83% of tumors with PVs and 7% with benign variants. These RPPVs represent a class of BRCA2 variants that have implications for the clinical management of carriers.

item.title: Gut microbiota GABA regulation by intestinal pH osmolality and microbial consumption
item.dc:creator: Kun Ye
Serafina Plüss
Claudia Moresi
Selma Aslani
Denisa Mujezinovic
Fabián A. Cornejo
Christophe Lacroix
Markus Arnoldini
item.description:
Authors: Kun Ye, Serafina Plüss, Claudia Moresi, Selma Aslani, Denisa Mujezinovic, Fabián A. Cornejo, Christophe Lacroix, Markus Arnoldini, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The production of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) by the gut microbiota has garnered attention due to its potential role as a driver of gut-brain axis signaling. However, mechanisms regulating microbiota-derived GABA under physiological conditions remain unclear. Here, we identified low pH and high osmolality as promoters of GABA production in the gut microbe Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron by driving changes in the expression of the glutamate decarboxylase system. pH also emerged as a critical factor for enhancing GABA production in a broader set of gut microbes. However, in the cecal microbiota of specific pathogen-free mice and in an ex vivo model of the human colon microbiota, GABA levels did not increase under physiologically relevant acidic conditions. This can partly be explained by microbial GABA consumption. Consistently, reducing cecal pH increased GABA levels in Oligo-MM 12 mice, a gnotobiotic model lacking GABA-consuming gut microbes. Our findings highlight the intricate balance between gut microbial GABA production, consumption, and environmental factors such as pH and osmolality.

item.title: Constructing radiative dipolar excitons via frontier-state hybridization in 2D perovskites
item.dc:creator: Jiakai Yan
Cheng Wang
Siyi Wu
Wei Dai
Shuwen Jia
Yan Zeng
Wenbo Li
Yan Li
item.description:
Authors: Jiakai Yan, Cheng Wang, Siyi Wu, Wei Dai, Shuwen Jia, Yan Zeng, Wenbo Li, Yan Li, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Realizing dipolar excitons that simultaneously exhibit strong optical activity and long-range repulsive interactions remains a central challenge in exciton-based nonlinear optics. This challenge stems from the intrinsic trade-off between achieving spatial charge separation, which is necessary for dipole formation, and maintaining sufficient wavefunction overlap to ensure efficient radiative recombination. Here, we overcome this trade-off in the two-dimensional perovskite (AE3T)PbI 4 by leveraging organic-inorganic band-edge engineering to induce frontier-state hybridization, thereby forming bright hybridized dipolar excitons with spatially indirect character and appreciable optical transition strength. These excitons combine an out-of-plane permanent electric-dipole component, room-temperature nonlinear transport consistent with long-range dipole–dipole repulsion, and finite optical transition dipole moments. Beyond addressing a key constraint in dipolar-exciton design, this work establishes frontier-state hybridization as a molecular design principle for constructing optically active, electrically polarized excitons in low-dimensional quantum materials.

item.title: Mapping redox networks in cardiomyocytes reveals non-overlapping response pathways for cytosolic versus mitochondrial H₂O₂ signaling
item.dc:creator: Yamin Chen
Juan Camilo Cárdenas-Arciniegas
Ana Maria Vergel Leon
Wiebke Maurer
Ayman Maher Ibrahim
Anke Zieseniss
Lesley Kurschat
Annette Hillemann
item.description:
Authors: Yamin Chen, Juan Camilo Cárdenas-Arciniegas, Ana Maria Vergel Leon, Wiebke Maurer, Ayman Maher Ibrahim, Anke Zieseniss, Lesley Kurschat, Annette Hillemann, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11756
Abstract: Abstract Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are essential redox messengers, yet their effects depend on concentration, localization, and duration. Here, we investigate how compartment-specific hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) production influences cardiomyocyte redox signaling and function. Using human induced pluripotent stem cell–derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CM) expressing the H₂O₂ biosensor HyPer fused to D-amino acid oxidase (DAO), we achieve chemogenetic control of H₂O₂ generation in the cytosol, mitochondria, or nucleus. Cytosolic H₂O₂ propagates throughout the cell, whereas mitochondrially generated H₂O₂ remains spatially restricted, reflecting compartmentalized antioxidant buffering. Cytosolic H₂O₂ impairs contractility and relaxation in both 2D and 3D engineered heart tissue models, accompanied by preferential oxidation of Z-disc–associated and actin-binding proteins and by altered sarcomere organization. Antioxidant treatment attenuates these effects. In contrast, mitochondrially produced H₂O₂ is better tolerated and associated with adaptive redox remodeling, with preserved contractile performance that is antagonized by conoidin A-induced inhibition of cytosolic peroxiredoxin activity. These findings demonstrate that the subcellular source of H₂O₂ shapes redox propagation, oxidation patterns, and functional responses, highlighting redox compartmentalization as a determinant of cardiomyocyte performance and stress resilience.

item.title: RSM01, an extended half-life RSV monoclonal antibody with a high barrier to in vitro resistance
item.dc:creator: Jonne Terstappen
Emanuele C. Gustani Buss
Cassandra A. L. Simonich

Vicky-Lynne Baillie

item.description:
Authors: Jonne Terstappen, Emanuele C. Gustani Buss, Cassandra A. L. Simonich, Jason S. McLellan, Vicky-Lynne Baillie, Jesse D. Bloom, Louis J. Bont, Mauricio T. Caballero, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes substantial infant morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). RSM01 is a long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody (mAb) in development for LMICs. In vitro generation of RSM01 resistant mutants has previously been unsuccessful. We systematically assessed the in vitro resistance barrier of RSM01 and the susceptibility of a panel of global contemporary strains to RSM01. Monoclonal antibody resistant mutants (MARMs) were generated by serially passaging triple plaque-purified RSV-A2 and RSV-B1 using HEp-2 cells under pressure from RSM01, nirsevimab, or palivizumab, followed by phenotypic and genotypic characterisation. Moderate resistance was defined as > 3-fold and high resistance as > 30-fold increase in IC 50 compared with parental virus. The susceptibility of contemporary global clinical strains to RSM01 was tested in a neutralisation assay. RSV-A and B strains developed high resistance to palivizumab and nirsevimab, while RSM01 pressure induced moderate resistance. No MARMs demonstrated a fitness advantage. RSM01 neutralised global contemporary strains. In conclusion, in vitro RSM01 resistance was infrequent and moderate and RSM01 had broad activity against circulating strains. The confirmation of the high barrier to resistance of RSM01 is encouraging and provides an alternative should resistance emerge with widespread use of current licensed anti-RSV mAbs.

item.title: Identification of translation events that drive nonsense-mediated mRNA decay reveals functional roles for alternative RNA isoforms
item.dc:creator: David J. Young
Yuejun Wang
Nicholas R. Guydosh
item.description:
Authors: David J. Young, Yuejun Wang, Nicholas R. Guydosh
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11755
Abstract: Abstract The nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway targets mRNAs undergoing premature translation termination for degradation. Previously, RNA-seq of yeast lacking NMD revealed that most genes targeted by NMD lack obvious premature termination codons (PTCs). We develop a combined approach using RNA-seq and 40S ribosome profiling to identify cryptic premature termination events that could account for NMD on nearly all these transcripts, including many alternative RNA transcript isoforms associated with annotated genes. Many NMD-targeted transcripts appear to be involved in two-promoter gene regulatory systems and share properties with long un-decoded transcript isoforms (LUTIs). In particular, we show that the DAL5 LUTI regulates expression of the DAL5 protein-coding mRNA in response to changes to environmental nitrogen. Our work expands the functional roles for LUTIs and establishes the importance of NMD in their regulation.

item.title: Staggered cryo-plasma FIB milling enables high-throughput cryo-ET
item.dc:creator: Elisa Lisicki
Tatjana Taubitz
Thorsten Wagner
Stefan Raunser
Sebastian Tacke
item.description:
Authors: Elisa Lisicki, Tatjana Taubitz, Thorsten Wagner, Stefan Raunser, Sebastian Tacke
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11758
Abstract: Abstract Cryo-focused ion beam (cryo-FIB) milling combined with cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is a crucial technique for studying macromolecules in their native environment. To mill thick samples, plasma ion sources are used. However, the practicality of high plasma currents, which offer the greatest potential for increasing throughput, and their possible damaging effects on the sample have not yet been investigated. Here, we systematically examine high-current xenon plasma-FIB (PFIB) milling and quantify the current-dependent damage in over 4700 tomograms by preparing a total lift-out volume of 9000 µm³. We find that currents of up to 2500 nA can be used in cryo-ET lamella preparations, enabling increased milling speeds and sample volumes that can be examined while maintaining sample integrity. We demonstrate this using a newly developed high-throughput staggered milling routine for waffle-like preparations, in which we achieve high-resolution reconstructions of yeast ribosomes, and for tissue serial lift-outs, enabling a complete experiment within 24 hours. Our results and approach provide a strong foundation for future in situ structural investigations of medically relevant protein complexes in organoids, tissues, or entire organisms.

item.title: Posterior alpha/beta oscillations reflect oculomotor dynamics underlying subsequent memory effects
item.dc:creator: Xiongbo Wu
Tzvetan Popov
Tara Beilner
Nicholas Fearns

item.description:
Authors: Xiongbo Wu, Tzvetan Popov, Tara Beilner, Nicholas Fearns, Christian Vollmar, Elisabeth Kaufmann, Jan Remi, Tobias Staudigl
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11750
Abstract: Abstract Neural activity and eye movements are well-established predictors of human memory performance. Successful memory formation is associated with reduced alpha/beta power and increased eye movements. However, their coupling and combined contribution to memory formation remain largely unknown. Across four experiments combining eye tracking with scalp or intracranial electroencephalography during free or constrained viewing, we identify the degree of visual exploration, rather than subsequent memory performance, as consistent modulator of posterior alpha/beta power. Going beyond correlations, manipulating eye movements dissociated alpha/beta power reductions from memory. Together with the finding that saccade parameters predicted alpha/beta dynamics, our results directly link posterior alpha/beta activity to the oculomotor system. Moreover, the accumulation of saccades over time accounted for reduced alpha/beta power, resembling the canonical post-stimulus alpha/beta pattern. Our work demonstrates that posterior alpha/beta activity strongly reflects eye movements, supporting alternative perspectives on alpha/beta subsequent memory effects and the general function of posterior alpha/beta activity.

item.title: Expansion of North Atlantic Deep Water during Northern Hemisphere Glaciation
item.dc:creator: Friso de Graaf
David Thornalley
David J. Wilson
Zarina Hewett
Yair Rosenthal
Stella Woodard
Heather L. Ford
item.description:
Authors: Friso de Graaf, David Thornalley, David J. Wilson, Zarina Hewett, Yair Rosenthal, Stella Woodard, Heather L. Ford
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major driver of the Earth’s climate, moving heat from the Southern Hemisphere to the Northern Hemisphere. Neither foraminiferal carbon isotope records nor modelling studies agree on the spatial extent of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), the northern deep limb of the AMOC, over the intensification of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (iNHG, ~2.73 million years ago). Here we present high-resolution neodymium isotope (ε Nd ) records from a depth transect in the equatorial Atlantic over the iNHG. We find a persistent latitudinal and depth gradient in neodymium isotope values in the deep Atlantic during the Late Pliocene, absent in the Early Pleistocene, indicating an expansion of NADW extent over the iNHG. In contrast, our reconstruction suggests very little glacial-interglacial variability in NADW extent during both the Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene. These results suggest deep-water circulation was substantially different during a warm climate state, with implications for the role of NADW formation during major climate transitions and its future stability.

item.dc:creator: Yanan Zhang
Xingpeng Yan
Jiaqi Li
Zijian Shi
Yang Yu
Yang Zhang
Tao Jing
item.description:
Authors: Yanan Zhang, Xingpeng Yan, Jiaqi Li, Zijian Shi, Yang Yu, Yang Zhang, Tao Jing
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Deep learning has advanced computer-generated holography, but learned models remain coupled to fixed wavelengths and distances, limiting generalization. Here we present the structurally guided wavefront neural encoder (SGWN-Encoder), which integrates diffraction physics with neural networks and employs a structural propagation strategy that analytically strips the parameter-sensitive global phase. This reveals a scale-normalized description of diffraction, letting the network learn transferable light-field evolution rules and generalize across propagation distances and visible wavelengths by direct inference. A dataset-free paradigm built on statistically diverse random fields teaches the model the structural mapping from complex amplitude to phase-only holograms instead of external image distributions. Without fine-tuning, a single SGWN-Encoder maintains a distance-averaged RGB PSNR of 31.9 dB and SSIM of 0.91 over the primary 2–200 mm range, retaining reconstruction up to 500 mm. Numerical and optical experiments on full-color 3D scenes establish a physically grounded route toward adaptive holographic displays.

item.title: A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures
item.dc:creator: Morihiro Ohta
Ching-Ping Lee
Vincent P. M. Sietses
I. Kostylev
J. R. Ball
P. Moroshkin

item.description:
Authors: Morihiro Ohta, Ching-Ping Lee, Vincent P. M. Sietses, I. Kostylev, J. R. Ball, P. Moroshkin, T. Hamamoto, Y. Kobayashi, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11458
Abstract: Abstract Current microwave quantum technologies require the amplification of weak signals with minimal added noise at millikelvin temperatures. To date, this stringent requirement has been met exclusively by superconducting technologies, such as Josephson or kinetic-inductance parametric amplifiers. A fundamentally distinct alternative approach could be offered by masers, the microwave counterpart of lasers, which were predicted as early as the 1950s to achieve quantum-limited noise performance under ideal conditions. However, their dependence on cryogenic operation historically limited further advancement. Here we demonstrate the first-ever non-superconducting, near-quantum-limited maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures utilising nitrogen impurity spins (P1 centres) in diamond. Population inversion is achieved via microwave pumping, exploiting a four-spin cross-relaxation mechanism. We realise a maximum power gain exceeding 30 dB, an added noise of approximately 2.55 quanta above the standard quantum limit, and a maximum 1 dB output compression point of −63 dBm at 6.595 GHz. The ability to operate in strong static magnetic fields of arbitrary orientation may offer a complementary, non-superconducting route for applications such as semiconducting spin-qubit readout, magnetic-resonance spectroscopy, and dark-matter axion searches.

Jarret A. P. Weinrich
Alyssa H. Marinas
Amanda Dombroski
Lain X. Pierce
Xilin Gu

item.description:
Authors: Matthew N. McCarroll, Jarret A. P. Weinrich, Alyssa H. Marinas, Amanda Dombroski, Lain X. Pierce, Xilin Gu, Megan J. Larmore, Jinfeng Teng, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract General anesthetics are essential for invasive medical procedures; however, there remains a need for safer agents. Using a bespoke 96-well-plate format platform enabling high-throughput imaging of larval zebrafish behavior, we screen 12,000 compounds and identify an isoxazole chemotype that phenocopies the intravenous anesthetics etomidate and propofol. Its optimization via medicinal chemistry yields an anesthetic that we call nidradine. This anesthetic is efficacious in both zebrafish and mice and lacks the problematic adrenal suppression characteristic of etomidate. Mechanistic studies using electrophysiology and structural biology reveal that nidradine, like etomidate and propofol, is a positive allosteric modulator of the GABA A receptor. Remarkably, behavioral assays in mice demonstrate that nidradine differs from most general anesthetics in that it also produces analgesia at subsedative doses.

item.title: Leveraging sequence purification for accurate prediction of multiple conformational states with AlphaFold2
item.dc:creator: Enming Xing
Junjie Zhang
Shen Wang
Xiaolin Cheng
item.description:
Authors: Enming Xing, Junjie Zhang, Shen Wang, Xiaolin Cheng
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract AlphaFold2 (AF2) has transformed protein structure prediction by harnessing co-evolutionary constraints embedded in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs). MSAs not only encode static structural information, but also contain evolutionary signatures linked to protein dynamics and conformational heterogeneity, which are central to biological function. However, the subtle co-evolutionary signals that bias proteins toward distinct conformational states are often obscured by noise within MSA data and remain challenging to decipher. Here, we introduce AF-ClaSeq, a systematic framework that enriches and purifies state-specific evolutionary signals through iterative sequence classification and selection. By identifying sequence subsets that preferentially encode distinct conformational states, AF-ClaSeq enables robust predictions of alternative conformations across diverse protein systems. Our findings indicate that the accuracy of alternative-state prediction depends more on the purity of the evolutionary signal within an MSA than on sequence depth. Notably, purified sequences encoding specific structural states are distributed across phylogenetic clades and superfamilies, rather than being confined to individual lineages. By extending AF2 beyond single-state structure prediction, AF-ClaSeq provides a promising approach for exploring protein structural plasticity, establishing a foundation for future studies of the sequence determinants underlying conformational switching and allosteric regulation.

item.dc:creator: Lauren M. Herr
Srijita Dhar

item.description:
Authors: Lauren M. Herr, Srijita Dhar, Martina Rossi, Ethan D. Schaffer, Kajal Biswas, Sandra S. Burkett, Ezgi Gül Keskin, Arindam Datta, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The mechanistic basis for chromosomal instability characteristic of RECQ helicase disorders remains poorly understood due to their molecular-genetic complexity. To characterize the genetic interactions of RECQL1 ( also referred to as RECQL or RECQ1) , implicated in RECON syndrome, we performed an RNA interference screen and discovered a functional relationship with BLM , a gene that is mutated in Bloom syndrome. RECQL1/BLM co-deficient cells display pronounced replication stress, DNA damage accumulation, and chromosomal instability. Strikingly, RECQL1/BLM co-deficiency induces sister chromatid separation during metaphase suppressible by depletion of the cohesin unloader WAPL, suggesting that a threshold of replication stress in the genetically co-deficient cells disrupts cohesion. Primary embryonic fibroblasts from transgenic Blm -/- ;Recql -/- mice recapitulate the sister chromatid separation phenotype and heightened replication stress observed for human cells. Our findings highlight the joint roles of RECQL1 and BLM in the replication stress response and their concurrent importance for maintenance of chromosomal stability even in the absence of exogenously induced DNA damage. Furthermore, we elucidated a genetic interaction in which sister chromatid cohesion is synergistically elevated by the loss of two conserved RECQ helicases encoded by genes in which mutations are linked to hereditary diseases that are not associated with sister chromatid cohesion defects. The findings presented provide insights into the genetic crosstalk of two prominent RECQ helicases with established importance in clinical diseases of genomic instability.

item.title: MyoGen: unified biophysical modeling of human neuromotor activity and resulting signals
item.dc:creator: Raul C. Sîmpetru
Ricardo G. Molinari
Devon R. Rohlf

item.description:
Authors: Raul C. Sîmpetru, Ricardo G. Molinari, Devon R. Rohlf, Rebeka L. Batichotti, Renato N. Watanabe, Leonardo A. Elias, Alessandro Del Vecchio
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11532
Abstract: Abstract Understanding human motor control requires integrating cortical and spinal activity, muscle mechanics, and electrophysiology, which are typically studied in isolation. We present MyoGen, an open-source framework that unifies spinal circuitry, proprioceptive feedback, musculotendon dynamics, and multimodal electromyography generation. Using data-driven optimization benchmarked against human motor unit recordings, MyoGen produces motor unit population activity matching experimental discharge-rate distributions and variability across muscles. The framework generates decomposable surface and intramuscular electromyography, reproduces beta-band modulation of descending drive and its transformation into force, and implements key sensorimotor loop components. Dimensionality reduction of simulated agonist-antagonist electromyography reveals low-dimensional control manifolds consistent with recordings from able-bodied individuals and those with spinal cord injury. Here, we show that MyoGen provides a physiologically grounded simulation substrate, enabling systematic investigation of motor control principles, benchmarking of signal-processing algorithms, and exploration of experimentally inaccessible sensorimotor interactions.

item.title: 4D mitochondrial network assumes distinct and predictive phenotypes through human lung and intestinal epithelial development
item.dc:creator: Gillian McMahon
Dhruv Agarwal
Mehul Arora
Zichen Wang

item.description:
Authors: Gillian McMahon, Dhruv Agarwal, Mehul Arora, Zichen Wang, Eric Arkfeld, Hiroyuki Hakozaki, Johannes Schöneberg
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Mitochondria form dynamic three-dimensional networks that exhibit a wide range of morphology and motility depending on cell state, cell type, and cell fate. Isolated phenotypes have been described for individual cell states, but how mitochondrial morphology and motility change across the full course of human tissue development has so far been unclear. Human stem cell-derived branching lung and intestinal organoids mimic developing human organs and make these systems accessible. Here we show, by imaging at key developmental time points from human stem cell through mature organoid tissue with lattice light-sheet microscopy, that mitochondrial networks adopt morphology and motility signatures that vary with developmental stage, that mitochondrial and cellular features can be used to predict developmental stage, and that two-dimensional measurements obscure features resolved only in three dimensions over time, yielding an integrated map of mitochondrial phenotypes across human tissue development.

item.title: Improving molecular property prediction with score-based diffusion models
item.dc:creator: Julien Horwood
Dino Oglic
José Miguel Hernández-Lobato
item.description:
Authors: Julien Horwood, Dino Oglic, José Miguel Hernández-Lobato
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract We explore diffusion-based training as a flexible approach to molecular property prediction in settings shaped by chemical, biophysical, and latent heterogeneity. To address this, we build on score-based generative diffusion models and introduce a conditional diffusion module for predictive tasks, equipped with a joint training and sampling guidance scheme and an optional gated residual mechanism that regulates feature- vs target-driven information flow across noise levels. The module acts as a plug-in learning block for existing molecular encoders, making it complementary to advances in representation learning. Across diverse feature extractors and graph neural networks, diffusion-based training improves over conventional maximum-likelihood objectives on small-molecule regression benchmarks and matches or exceeds strong baselines on multitask regression and classification datasets. It also produces well-calibrated predictive uncertainty as measured by prediction interval coverage, enables confidence-guided ranking, and performs well in challenging settings including activity cliffs and class-imbalanced multitask prediction. Overall, these results position diffusion as a promising representation-agnostic approach for effective molecular property prediction.

item.title: Rhizospheric pH mediated thermo-signalling coordinates root growth under heat stress
item.dc:creator: Aneesh S. Lale
Atish Bansod
Srija Chakraborty
Erfan Ghafouri
Jayne L. Davis
Thanh B. Nghiem
Feijian Sun
Brighton Gapare
item.description:
Authors: Aneesh S. Lale, Atish Bansod, Srija Chakraborty, Erfan Ghafouri, Jayne L. Davis, Thanh B. Nghiem, Feijian Sun, Brighton Gapare, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Heat stress events pose a major threat to global agriculture due to elevated air and soil temperatures. While plant roots regulate their growth in response to elevated soil temperatures, they appear to rely on thermosensory mechanisms distinct from those used by shoots. Here, we report pH as a key component of a thermo-signaling mechanism that regulates temperature-dependent root responses via ROS-mediated control of cell cycle dynamics in Arabidopsis thaliana . At moderately high temperatures, alkalization of meristematic and transition zones increases superoxide (O₂⁻) levels, promoting cell division and root growth. Conversely, higher temperatures inhibit growth by increasing acidification and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) accumulation in these zones. Elevating external pH buffers this acidification, reduces H₂O₂ levels, and confers heat resistance. Our data support that this pH-mediated heat resistance is also effective under soil conditions. The heat-induced pH shifts are controlled by plasma membrane H⁺-ATPases (PM-H⁺-ATPases), which are under the control of the kinases TOT3 and TOI5. Our findings reveal an interesting pathway for plant adaptation to heat stress, linking pH, ROS and root thermomorphogenesis, with major implications for improving plant resilience in warming climates.

item.title: Assembly of a renal countercurrent system in a beetle
item.dc:creator: Robin Beaven
Mila Fafinska
Jian Dai
Kenneth V. Halberg
Barry Denholm
item.description:
Authors: Robin Beaven, Mila Fafinska, Jian Dai, Kenneth V. Halberg, Barry Denholm
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Countercurrent exchange describes the crossover of some property between two bodies flowing in opposite direction. Countercurrent circuits, which work more efficiently than concurrent circuits, are common in nature and mimicked in human engineering. An example is the beetle cryptonephridial complex (CNC)—a multi-organ water conservation system which makes key contributions to the water budget in a vast number of species. It is even used by some to harvest water from the atmosphere. The system evolved by a radical reorganisation of insect internal anatomy bringing the renal/Malpighian tubules and rectum into countercurrent configuration, and their isolation in a chamber by an unusual tissue of unknown origin—the perinephric membrane. The CNC is richly supplied with tracheae to meet the high metabolic demands of the system. How the CNC is assembled during development is unknown. Here we characterise CNC development in the model beetle Tribolium castaneum and discover the molecular signals orchestrating its assembly. We find that dynamic crosstalk between the developing precursor cells of the rectum, Malpighian tubules, perinephric membrane, and trachea rely on a single, differentially spliced fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor and two FGF pathway ligands. We also map the origin of the perinephric membrane to a previously uncharacterised population of mesodermal cells, providing clues to its evolutionary origin. This work illuminates the developmental processes underpinning the reorganisation of the insect internal body plan to assemble a natural countercurrent system, one which is fundamental to beetle physiology, ecology and evolutionary success.

item.title: Directly visualizing the energy level structure of quantum dot molecules
item.dc:creator: Heun Mo Yoo
Tanner M. Janda
Connor Nasseraddin
Jason R. Petta
item.description:
Authors: Heun Mo Yoo, Tanner M. Janda, Connor Nasseraddin, Jason R. Petta
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The orbital, spin and valley degrees of freedom in silicon quantum dots (QDs) support many modes of spin qubit operation. However, it is generally challenging to probe the energy level spectrum over a large parameter space. We demonstrate a spectroscopic technique capable of mapping the energy level structure of a double quantum dot as a function of level detuning, interdot tunnel coupling, and magnetic field. In the one-electron regime, we directly observe the transition from the atom-like energy levels of isolated QDs to molecular-like bonding and anti-bonding states with increasing interdot tunnel coupling. We also resolve the Zeeman splitting of ground and excited valley states in a magnetic field. In the two-electron regime, we gain access to the detuning dependent singlet-triplet splitting. Our work may be extended to a broader class of systems, such as strong spin-orbit materials or proximitized QDs, allowing the direct extraction of various energy gaps.

item.title: Molecular profiling of repeated self-sampled blood reveals dynamic immune phenotypes in young adults
item.dc:creator: Annika Bendes
Sophia Björkander
Maura M. Kere
Simon Kebede Merid

item.description:
Authors: Annika Bendes, Sophia Björkander, Maura M. Kere, Simon Kebede Merid, Ashish Kumar, Leo Dahl, Tess D. Pottinger, Zhebin Yu, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11680
Abstract: Abstract Although population-based studies of circulating blood proteins have provided profound insight into human biology, transient changes to time-dependent exposures often remain elusive. Here, we perform a longitudinal dried blood spot (DBS) self-sampling study in 808 young adults (aged 24–27, 64% females) from the Swedish Barn [Children], Allergy, Milieu, Stockholm Epidemiology cohort. In total, we collected ~2400 samples from 2020 to 2022. Each sample was profiled for SARS-CoV-2 serological, anti-interferon autoantibodies (AAbs), and 365 inflammation-related proteins. We subsequently linked these samples to registry-confirmed infection and vaccination exposures, physiological traits, genetic variation, and blood counts. We show that data-driven seroclustering captures the response to both infection and vaccination exposures, while stable AAbs against interferon receptors IFNAR1 and IFNGR2 associate with the duration of self-reported COVID-19 symptoms. Genome-wide mapping reveals 664 protein quantitative trait loci (pQTL) across 65 proteins, with cis -pQTLs associated proteins showing greater longitudinal stability. Paired pre- and post-exposure samples indicate temporal changes in protein levels after infection (LAP3) and vaccination (TIMP3). This multi-molecular epidemiological profiling of self-sampled blood captures dynamic immune trajectories and shorter-term variability in a population of young adults.

item.title: Theoretical frameworks for credit assignment via behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity
item.dc:creator: Ian Cone
Claudia Clopath
Rui Ponte Costa
item.description:
Authors: Ian Cone, Claudia Clopath, Rui Ponte Costa
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Behavioral Timescale Synaptic Plasticity (BTSP) is a form of plasticity which drives place field formation in hippocampal pyramidal neurons. Unlike traditional learning rules, BTSP learns pre-post correlations on timescales of seconds and rapidly changes single-unit activity in only a few trials. To study how BTSP-like learning can be integrated into network models, we propose a generalized theoretical framework, gBTSP, which we apply to unsupervised and supervised tasks in feedforward and recurrent networks. We show that unsupervised gBTSP learns place field maps in the feedforward case and attractor memories in the recurrent case. For supervised learning, we derive how plateau events can reduce task error, enabling gBTSP to solve trajectory matching and delayed non-match-to-sample tasks. Finally, we find that the speed of credit assignment via gBTSP is limited by network depth or CA3-like recurrence, suggesting that additional mechanisms are necessary to account for BTSP-driven few-shot learning in naturalistic settings.

item.title: Chirality-locked low-dimensional bound states in the continuum lasers
item.dc:creator: Heegeun Kim
Chiwon Shin
Seunghoon Bae
Kyoung-Ho Kim
Hong-Gyu Park
item.description:
Authors: Heegeun Kim, Chiwon Shin, Seunghoon Bae, Kyoung-Ho Kim, Hong-Gyu Park
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Bound states in the continuum (BICs) support high-quality-factor resonances embedded in extended spectra, and their radiation properties can be tailored through perturbative symmetry breaking and chiral engineering. However, because BICs are intrinsically delocalized states of infinite periodic structures, they typically require large spatial footprints. Achieving localized BIC modes while preserving radiation suppression and topological singularities, and simultaneously enabling chiral responses, remains a challenge. Here, we experimentally realize low-threshold BIC lasers localized at one-dimensional interfaces and zero-dimensional junctions by interfacing domains with identical bulk BIC characteristics but opposite chirality. The resulting interfaces and junctions host spatially localized states that exhibit optical spin–momentum-locked emission governed by the assigned chirality, while retaining intrinsic BIC properties, including narrow far-field divergence and pump-selective lasing localization. In addition, polarization singularities confirm the topological nature of these low-dimensional BICs, particularly the well-defined topological charge of the zero-dimensional junction mode. Coupling two zero-dimensional BICs further gives rise to bonding and antibonding supermodes, enabling non-Hermitian, chirality-locked behaviors. These results establish a route to compact, high-quality-factor photonic states with engineered chirality through dimensional reduction of BICs, without relying on defect confinement or band inversion.

item.title: Functional diversity of GPCR–Gustducin complexes controls signaling output and suppresses alternative pathways
item.dc:creator: Victoria Jaime Arce
Mira Lettmann
Mona Stefanie Tögl
Santiago Javier Bonn Garcia
Max Bauer
Maike Neukirch

item.description:
Authors: Victoria Jaime Arce, Mira Lettmann, Mona Stefanie Tögl, Santiago Javier Bonn Garcia, Max Bauer, Maike Neukirch, Olivia Kleinstück, Anastasia Langolf, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11681
Abstract: Abstract Gustducin (G gust ), the G protein mediating taste receptor signaling, is expressed not only in sensory taste cells but throughout the human body alongside numerous non-taste G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). Whether and how these receptors engage G gust , and the functional consequences of such interactions, remain poorly understood. Here, we develop two complementary biosensors that enable direct monitoring of GPCR–G gust interaction and downstream signaling in living cells, allowing pharmacological characterization of G gust activity induced by non-taste GPCRs. We find that several non-taste GPCRs do not activate G gust but instead stabilize the G protein heterotrimer and suppress basal signaling by forming unproductive GPCR–G protein complexes, whereas others induce conventional G gust activation and signal transduction. We further show that these unproductive GPCR–G gust complexes suppress the activation of alternative signaling pathways by sequestering receptors from other G proteins. This mode of interaction functionally partitions GPCRs into activators and inactivators of G gust and represents a mechanism for balancing concurrent signaling pathways within a cell.

item.description:
Authors: Joshua A. Brown, Yijia Ma, Yifan Wang, John J. Massa, Peter Kuan-Hao Cheng, Chaowen Chen, Mingzhou Ding, Norman B. Schmidt, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract How transient threats turn into persistent, long-term fear memories is a fundamental problem in neuroscience, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Early sensory cortex, traditionally viewed as a passive feature analyzer, is increasingly recognized as an active participant in fear processing. Combining high-definition α-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (HD α-tACS) with simultaneous EEG-fMRI (electroencephalography-functional magnetic resonance imaging) and transformer-based neural decoding, we tracked fear memory development across formation, consolidation, and long-term retention (assessed at 15 min, 24 h, and 7 days after fear conditioning). Spatiotemporal memory traces were identified at all three assessments, beginning at an early sensory stage (40–60 ms post-stimulus) and distributed across visual cortex and limbic regions. Conditioning potentiated occipital α-oscillation desynchronization, a marker of visual cortical disinhibition, which subsequently predicted the strength of long-term memory traces. Critically, targeted α-tACS over early visual cortex induced early visual cortical (V1/V2) inhibition, abolished conditioning-potentiated α desynchronization, and selectively disrupted fear-memory consolidation and retention while leaving initial acquisition intact. These findings establish sensory cortical disinhibition as a necessary mechanism for long-term fear memory in humans and identify early sensory cortex as crucial node for intervention of persistent maladaptive fear.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a complex autoimmune disease with a substantial heritable component. We perform multi-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analyses of 351,498 individuals (comprising 39,600 RA cases and 311,898 controls) by integrating published and new datasets. This analysis identifies 29 novel RA susceptibility loci and systematically classifies association signals as population-specific, population-dominant, or population-shared between East Asian and European populations. Bayesian fine-mapping and functional annotation prioritize putative causal variants, highlighting 67 variants with posterior inclusion probability>0.1 in novel loci, including an SLC27A6 missense variant (rs137898880) and a STIM1 3′ UTR variant (rs3750996). Our gene-prioritization framework combining genetic and biological evidence identifies 203 high-confidence effector genes, 16 of which reside in novel loci (e.g., IFI16 , AIM2 , RGS1 , ITPKB , CD80 , RHOH , NFKB1 , SIK3 , and CCND2 ). Colocalization analysis leveraging tissue-specific eQTL datasets provides mechanistic insights by implicating shared causal variants underlying RA association signals. Notably, the transcription factor gene RUNX3 at a novel locus shows evidence of cis -regulation in immune cells, and RUNX3-binding sites are enriched for variants explaining excess RA heritability, suggesting a potential role for RUNX3 as a trans -regulatory mediator of RA risk at distal RA loci. Finally, exploratory gene-drug interaction networks weighted by RA association strength highlight population-informed therapeutic opportunities and drug-repurposing targets driven largely by novel loci.

Abstract: Abstract Advances in cryoEM have led to a surge in high-resolution structures; however, model building and refinement at resolutions ( > = 3 Å) and in regions with variable local resolution remain challenging, making validation essential. CryoEM derived assemblies often contain extensive protein-protein interfaces, however, most existing validation metrics focus on density fit or overall geometry without directly assessing interface quality. To address this, we present DPI-Score, a deep learning-based metric for assessing protein-protein interfaces in cryoEM derived complexes. The method uses only raw structural coordinates of interface atoms, without requiring engineered features, and achieves 87.53% validation accuracy. DPI-Score was applied to 29,120 interfaces from 6,011 fitted entries with resolutions worse than 3 Å in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank. Here, we show that DPI-Score provides complementary information to existing validation metrics and can identify interface errors in modelled assemblies that are not detected by density-based scores alone.

item.description:
Authors: Ian M. Hayes, Elliot Fang, Shanta R. Saha, Vivek Mishra, P. J. Hirschfeld, Johnpierre Paglione
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract One of the recurring hurdles in studying unconventional superconductivity is the challenge of efficiently and conclusively identifying the symmetry of the superconducting order parameter in a new material. Uranium ditelluride (UTe 2 ) exhibits an unprecedented number of superconducting phases, and none of them has had its symmetry conclusively identified so far. Here we report results of an extensive study of the thermal conductivity of UTe 2 in the superconducting state as a function of the angle of an applied magnetic field rotated in the b-c plane. We observe substantial oscillations in the thermal conductivity as a function of field angle, and, utilizing the experimentally determined Fermi surface, we model this phenomenon for all potential gap structures in UTe 2 . This allows us to identify point nodes near the b-axis, implying that the superconducting order parameter most likely belongs to the B 2 u irreducible representation of the crystal point group.

Authors: Shuto Suzuki, Kosuke Nakayama, Koki Yanagizawa, Katsuaki Sugawara, Seigo Souma, Kenichi Ozawa, Shunichi Takano, Ryoga Takahara, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11407
Abstract: Abstract Layered transition-metal dichalcogenide 1T-TaS 2 has long been considered a prime example of a Mott insulator driven by strong electron correlations. However, this view has been recently challenged by proposals which favor a band insulating state arising from interlayer dimerization. This ongoing debate opens a frontier in 1T-TaS 2 research focusing on stacking order, and raises a fundamental question with broad implications for two-dimensional materials: can electronic phases be engineered by actively tuning interlayer coupling? Here, using micro-focused angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy supported by first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that uniaxial strain drives 1T-TaS 2 from its insulating charge-density-wave phase into a stable metallic phase. This metallic phase, distinct from hydrostatic-pressure-induced or non-equilibrium hidden phases, emerges via a strain-induced rearrangement in the interlayer stacking of the Star-of-David charge order, effectively disrupting interlayer dimerization. Furthermore, the emergent metallic phase exhibits a significant quasiparticle mass renormalization, a hallmark of strong electron correlations, indicating its correlated nature and proximity to a Mott instability. This finding necessitates a re-evaluation of the interplay between structural and strong correlations in 1T-TaS 2 . The present results establish uniaxial strain as a powerful method for tuning the interlayer coupling, opening pathways for exploring quantum phases inaccessible under ambient conditions.

Abstract: Abstract High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves ~ 300 nm lateral and ~ 650 nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and < 60 nm localization precision in vivo. Compared with two-photon point scanning, the lower illumination NA delivers order-of-magnitude lower peak intensity, enabling > 5 × faster volumetric acquisition (up to 3.25 × 10 6 voxels s −1 ). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by ~ 2 × and restores volumetric resolving power by > 2 × relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

Authors: YoungJu Park, Taegil Kim, Jonghyeok Baek, Seongbin Park, Daeho Kim, ChaeHo Shin, Sokhuoy Sam, Wonyoung Kim, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Intramolecular charge transport is conventionally described as proceeding along a static ground-state potential, with the carrier acting as a passive probe of a fixed electronic landscape. Here, using alkanethiolate-based molecular junctions, we show that the carrier itself can drive conformational reorganization once the applied bias brings backbone-delocalized molecular orbitals into the transmission window. Combined electrical and in situ structural measurements resolve a threshold-activated transition to a gauche-defect state coincident with the onset of orbital-mediated transport. We rationalize this coupling through a quantum resonance scattering framework in which accessible orbitals act as scattering potentials that transiently host the injected charge, depositing energy into nuclear motion with an efficiency set by molecule–electrode coupling and Franck–Condon overlap. The framework quantitatively reproduces the measured response and predicts the enhanced behavior of amide-containing junctions. Together, these results suggest that charge-transport–structure feedback can be understood in terms of microscopic parameters governing resonance-mediated energy transfer, and that these parameters may be tuned through chemical design.

Abstract: Abstract Immunocompromised adults are at increased risk of severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) disease. This multicountry, open-label phase 2b trial (NCT05921903) evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of the AS01 E -adjuvanted RSV prefusion F protein vaccine (adjuvanted RSVPreF3) over 12 months in kidney or lung transplant recipients ≥18 years, randomized 1:1 to receive one ( n = 131) or two doses 30–60 days apart ( n = 130). The primary outcome was the mean geometric increase in RSV-A and RSV-B neutralizing titers one month following a second adjuvanted RSVPreF3 dose relative to the first dose in transplant recipients. Secondary outcomes included assessment of the safety and immunogenicity of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in transplant recipients compared with the control group. In transplant recipients receiving two doses, neutralizing titers against RSV-A and RSV-B were numerically higher one month post-dose 2 than post-dose 1 (mean geometric increases: 1.34 [95% CI: 1.20, 1.48] for RSV-A [ n = 111] and 1.26 [95% CI: 1.14, 1.40] for RSV-B [ n = 111]). Abstract: Abstract Early-life nutritional conditions may influence biological aging and age-related health, but the long-term associations of early exposure to sugar rationing remain unclear. Abstract: Abstract Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are promising laser-gain media for their direct bandgap and strong excitonic effects. However, existing TMD lasers typically rely on mechanically exfoliated or high-temperature chemical-vapor-deposition-grown materials, with their atomic-scale thickness inherently limiting the available optical gain volume. Using solution exfoliation and spray coating under ambient conditions, we produce area- and thickness-scalable BM-MoS 2 films composed of electronically decoupled MoS 2 monolayers separated by organic spacers. This layered architecture preserves the intrinsic monolayer excitonic properties while providing a tunable gain volume beyond that of an isolated monolayer. Integrated with WGM cavities, the thickness-scalable BM-MoS 2 films enable a balance between the quality ( Q ) and optical confinement ( $$\varGamma$$ Γ ) factors. Power-dependent measurements reveal key lasing signatures, including a threshold-like input-output crossover accompanied by linewidth narrowing at a pump power of approximately 1.4 nW, and pump-induced polarization selection. Abstract: Abstract The Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) recruits Mini-Chromosome Maintenance (MCM) hexamers to initiate eukaryotic DNA replication. While yeast ORC binds specific DNA motifs, human ORC binds sequence-agnostically nucleosome-depleted promoter regions. Here, using a mutant yeast model that recapitulates the human ORC binding landscape, we demonstrate that pervasive and unscheduled ORC binding at promoters in the compact yeast genome generates R-loop associated transcription-replication conflicts and disrupts gene expression across thousands of genes. Unexpectedly, we also uncover that substituting endogenous gene promoters with a replication origin sequence maintains robust transcription. We reveal that this intrinsic, promoter-like function relies on the ability of origins to form a nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) encoded within the origin’s sequence composition. However, origin-substituted loci reposition the +1 nucleosome which drives the transcription machinery to select alternative transcription start sites (TSSs). Thus, origins and promoters share an intrinsic chromatin structure-controlled ability to drive transcription initiation. Together, our results show that origin licensing in compact genomes relies on sequence-specific, coupled origin licensing to insulate transcription from the replication machinery.
